title: The Jacksonville Job: a touchdown that wasn't
summary: Down 20–6 with 12:26 left, Jacksonville appeared to score on Parker Washington’s end-zone catch. Officials ruled it incomplete and upheld the call; the Jaguars settled for three and ultimately lost 23–18.
preview: CBS rules analyst Gene Steratore thought Washington had a touchdown. The NFL said control was not established until out of bounds.

timeline.label: Early fourth quarter · 12:26 left
timeline.text: Trailing 20–6, Jacksonville faced third-and-9 at the Giants' 12. Trevor Lawrence found Parker Washington at the back of the end zone; the on-field ruling was incomplete.

timeline.label: Replay review
timeline.text: Liam Coen challenged. Replay upheld the incompletion. CBS rules analyst Gene Steratore said he believed Washington maintained control.

timeline.label: League explanation
timeline.text: NFL VP of instant replay Mark Butterworth said the ball shifted when Washington hit the ground and control was not established in bounds.

timeline.label: What it changed
timeline.text: A touchdown plus extra point would have cut the deficit to 20–13. Jacksonville kicked a field goal instead, making it 20–9; the Giants eventually won 23–18.

timeline.label: Other disputed decisions
timeline.text: Reports also questioned the Giants' Jameis Winston quarterback-sneak touchdown and a first-down spot reversed by replay assist before Jacksonville successfully challenged.

timeline.label: Hours later · Sunday Night Football
timeline.text: San Francisco's Mike Evans was credited with a one-handed touchdown against Minnesota despite NBC rules analyst Terry McAulay questioning whether Evans controlled the ball before going out of bounds. The on-field ruling differed from Washington's, and both stood; the plays are a comparison of officiating consistency, not proof of a coordinated fix.

timeline.label: A Giant raises the Vegas question
timeline.text: Giants safety Jevón Holland said he thought Washington might have caught the ball and jokingly said 'Shoutout Vegas' after the game. The remark was not an allegation backed by evidence.

unusual: A potentially comeback-changing touchdown was denied despite a national broadcast rules analyst disagreeing; other rulings during the same game also drew scrutiny.
explanations: The league defended its interpretation of possession and the standard for overturning the on-field ruling. Jacksonville also committed turnovers and missed other opportunities, so the disputed call cannot by itself establish who would have won.
questions: Was Washington in control before he went out of bounds?
Why did the broadcast analyst and replay office interpret the same video differently?
Did the sequence of rulings disproportionately hurt Jacksonville, or were these independent judgments?
Why did similar-looking catches involving Washington and Evans receive different on-field rulings that both survived replay?
